entries.title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn
entries.summary: Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlightsThe Disappearers by Marlon JamesHamish Hamilton, 3 September After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophob
entries.content:
Fiction

The Disappearers by Marlon James

Hamish Hamilton, 3 September

After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.

The Bridge by Colm Tóibín

Picador, 3 September

Twenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.

The Golden Hours by Louisa Young

Mantle, 3 September

Young continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.

Switzy by Emma Cline

Chatto & Windus, 10 September

With dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.

The Rouse by China Miéville

Picador, 17 September

A leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.

The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain

Chatto & Windus, 17 September

An origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.

Stations by Louise Kennedy

Bloomsbury, 24 September

The author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.

Doom Painting by AK Blakemore

Granta, 24 September

One of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.

American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee

4th Estate, 29 September

The hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.

Partita by Barbara Kingsolver

Faber, 6 October

After the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.

Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger

Jonathan Cape, 13 October

Set a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.

Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus

Manilla, 13 October

In the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.

In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak

Viking, 15 October

From the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.

Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li

4th Estate, 22 October

Set at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.

Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe

Viking, 12 November

Music is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.

Crime and thrillers

Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley return

Autumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. In Cold Sunset (Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise: We Chase Shadows (Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder in The Silent Appeal (Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.

Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction in The Heights (Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: in The Taper Man (Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.

Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthology Sherlock (Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.

Nonfiction

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer

Penguin Michael Joseph, 22 September

Thirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.

The Castle by Jon Ronson

Viking, 20 August

A concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.

The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown

Simon & Schuster, 1 September

The former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.

The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet

Hodder & Stoughton, 10 September

The queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.

Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History by Lucy Worsley

Hodder & Stoughton, 3 September

The historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.

All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci

Bodley Head, 17 September

Not many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.

End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor

Allen Lane, 15 September

Thinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.

Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond

Mariner, 22 September

The author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?

An Unexpected Life: A Memoir by Gloria Steinem

Ebury, 22 September

A totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.

Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo

John Murray, 24 September

In the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.

The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm Gladwell

Abacus, 29 September

The author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.

Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis

Allen Lane, 6 October

Lewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.

Requiem for Gaza by Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges

Jonathan Cape, 8 October

The master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.

The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick

Grand Central Publishing, 8 October

The NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.

Promise Me, America by Joe Biden

John Murray, 17 November

A year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.

Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg

Corsair, 5 November

The former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.

Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Art of Whitney Houston by Emily Lordi

White Rabbit, 1 October

English professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.

Memoir

From Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out for

It’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’s One Helluva Ride (Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’s The Steps (Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, try Fictional Selves by Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoir Look at Me (Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoir Secrets (Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career in Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? (Michael Joseph, 22 October). In Vigilauntie (W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who in The Queerest of Folk (Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political in How I’ve Tried to Change the World (W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines in Battle Axe (William Collins, 10 September).

entries.title: Alice Roberts: ‘By the time I’d finished Richard Dawkins I’d left faith behind’
entries.summary: The TV presenter and author on the evolutionary biologists who inspired her, the genius of George Eliot – and fun with Frog and ToadMy earliest reading memoryThe first books I remember were from The Village with Three Corners series Sheila K McCullagh. entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

The first books I remember were from The Village with Three Corners series Sheila K McCullagh. I loved the – literally – colourful characters, like Johnny Yellow Hat. I was reading with my Grandma, in her garden perhaps, sitting on a small patio, surrounded by bright begonias and busy lizzies.

My favourite book growing up

Arnold Lobel’s wonderful Frog and Toad stories. Toad would get himself tied up in knots, trying to find a button or fly a kite, but Frog was always there – a constant, caring and funny friend. I enjoyed reading these stories to my own children when they were young, and we still sometimes go back and revisit them. They’re so full of humour, heart and simple humanism.

The book that changed me as a teenager

At that time I loved Alan Garner, Susan Cooper and Rosemary Sutcliff. But the book I remember having a really profound effect on me was Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene. I was passionate about biology, and the gene’s-eye view turned it upside down and suddenly evolution made sense. I went on to voraciously read all of Stephen Jay Gould’s essays on evolutionary biology. Those two authors really inspired me.

The writer who changed my mind

When I picked up Dawkins’s The Blind Watchmaker, I was already beginning to seriously doubt the Anglican faith I’d been brought up in. By the time I finished it, I knew I’d left that faith behind. Biological diversity could be entirely explained through natural processes; there was no need for – and no evidence of – a divine creator. I became a humanist, although I didn’t know the word for it back then.

The book that made me want to be a writer

I never set out to be a writer. I wrote my first book as a handout to go with the first television series I wrote and presented on my own – Don’t Die Young on BBC Two. As a university academic, I wanted there to be something more to go with the programmes. I’d written papers of course, but nothing for a general readership, and I loved doing that. In my writing, whether that’s books or scripts for television and live shows, I always go back to Gould’s advice and example. He was adamant that it was possible to communicate complex ideas without “dumbing down” – you just need enough steps, and to strip away unnecessary jargon.

The book I came back to

One I keep coming back to – and this isn’t surprising for any biologist – is Darwin’s On the Origin of Species by Natural Selection. It’s so full of wonderful details and insights – and I love the way he takes his readers on a journey, from the known and familiar, to the novel and strange.

The book I discovered later in life

George Eliot’s Middlemarch – I only really sat down to read it five years ago. I never got on with the Brontë sisters or Jane Austen at school, and in my head, I’d put Eliot away on the same shelf labelled “novels that were boring and banal but got away with it because they were early examples of the genre and so there wasn’t much competition”! It was Andrew Copson, chief executive of Humanists UK, who finally persuaded me to read Middlemarch and I was blown away by it – the complexity of the characters and the way it challenges your prejudices. It is a masterpiece.

The book I am currently reading

For work I’m dipping into Fritz Graf’s Roman Festivals in the Greek East and Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price’s two volume series on the Religions of Rome. For pleasure, I have recently finished Val McDermid’s fabulous Queen Macbeth, and Karen Hao’s fascinating and troubling Empire of AI. I’m also listening to Otto English’s brilliant Notorious audiobook. And I am enjoying reading Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem to my teenage son – who still enjoys a bedtime story!

My comfort read

The Little Book of Humanism – a book I helped to compile, full of wonderful, everyday humanist wisdom.

entries.title: Life of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman?
entries.summary: A teasing tale of the friendship between a writer and an actor explores the fallout from fame, and the blurring between pretence and realityM is a celebrated film actor. entries.content:
M is a celebrated film actor. A star since childhood, now the face of a major fashion brand, she has been famous all her life. That her career closely resembles Natalie Portman’s has been gleefully seized upon by the press, something Rachel Cusk must surely have anticipated: in the novel, M’s first film has its sex scenes cut at her mother’s insistence, as happened with Portman’s 1994 debut Leon, while her ballerina movie is recognisably Black Swan. M is also, in the words of the nameless and genderless narrator of Life of M, “a good sport”. When the narrator suggests writing M’s autobiography, M likes the idea. “Would you just make it up?” she asks.

A celebrity autobiography is seldom the work of the celebrity herself. And yet any suggestion that the narrator will serve as a kind of ghostwriter to M is dispensed with in a few pages. The pair meet for coffee at a luxury hotel and, after the narrator’s partner falls suddenly and seriously ill, for lunch in a restaurant. The lunch is unsatisfactory, an attempt at intimacy that the narrator acknowledges afterwards to have been a mistake. Though M is determined to live as normal a life as possible (“her personal task is to become real, or rather to acquire some reality”), the narrator is uncomfortably aware of their own falseness with M: “It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real. It was as if she was the only one good enough at acting to attain reality.” After that the two of them do not see one another again “for a long time”.

And yet a book about M, or at least partly about M, materialises. Episodes from M’s life are intercut with observations from the narrator’s own experiences. The M sections are precise, specific: an acting class led by a renowned theatre director, a difficult encounter with a controlling ex, a holiday in an immaculately curated villa in Greece. The impression is of clips from a film, an effect heightened by the meticulous descriptions of place that preface each scene like the stage directions from a script, detailing everything from furniture and layout to the specific texture of the artificial wood floor in a five-star hotel suite. In a world where everyone is acting, Cusk seems to be saying, the appearance of things is all the certainty we have.

In this post-saturation era of social media exposure, the intersection of appearance and authenticity has been exhaustively picked over. Cusk’s insights are not strikingly new. Her power lies in the authority of her sharp, spare prose, the glittering exactness of her sentences. She writes with crisp acuity about the frictionless (and therefore strangely lifeless) existence of the celebrity, the corrosive effect of fame on family relationships, the blend of fervent purity and crushing cynicism that delimits a person forged in the forcefields of power and pretence. At Cusk’s startling best, and there is a good deal of that here, her ideas land like punches or uncomfortable secrets muttered in our ears: it is a shock to realise that they are our secrets too.

Life of M, like Cusk’s previous novel Parade, grew out of a piece published in the New Yorker, in this case a powerful short story titled Project. While the story has made its way almost whole into the opening chapters, the larger scope of the novel form gives Cusk the space to explore M more deeply. She may have famously declared in 2018 that “I don’t think character exists any more” but, stripped though her work is of the ordinary conventions of character and plot, her ideas land with greatest impact when they are rooted in the particular: a flaming sunset reflected on a switched-off television screen, a room in a museum meticulously curated to give the impression of a lived-in space, an “indifferent” fan approaching M for a selfie “as though M were a tourist monument”. M’s most compelling scenes, like those told to Faye in Cusk’s celebrated Outline trilogy, thrum with detail.

Faye was a deliberate absence, a vessel for other people’s stories. The narrator of Life of M is more a mirrored surface, their reflection of M’s celebrity as much a part of the illusion as the celebrity itself. What begins with a first-person singular narrator quickly morphs into a plural “we” which sometimes appears to represent the narrator and their partner, sometimes a more public “we”, both the counterpoint to and the rapaciously hungry engine for fame. Perhaps Cusk intends to co-opt the reader, to make us complicit. Perhaps she means to throw us off balance. What is certain is that the prose in these sections has an epigrammatic absolutism that, while occasionally brilliant (“We do not, as we did when we were young, see the evening as a mysterious kingdom in which we might meet our destiny”), is more often puzzlingly specific. How is it that “we” visit the apartment of a psychic with “frazzled hair” or recall that “our longest relationship was with someone who now frightens us”? It is not always clear what these parts add to the whole. Jokes, a reliably dark pleasure in Cusk’s work, are in regrettably short supply. Life of M is powered by a formidable intelligence and shaped with exceptional technical skill, at its best it leaves one reeling, but the impression it leaves is one of detachment, even disdain. It is a book to admire enormously, but not one to love.

entries.title: The best recent translated fiction – review roundup
entries.summary: The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio; Short Circuit by Wolf Haas; Cosmos by Lucia Odoom; The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra KamiyaThe Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio, translated by Mia Spangenberg, Penguin Classics (£14.99)Following Lowest Common Denominator and Backlight, this book completes Finnish author Saisio’s autofictional trilogy. It covers her young adulthood i
entries.content:
The Red Book of Farewells by Pirkko Saisio, translated by Mia Spangenberg, Penguin Classics (£14.99)

Following Lowest Common Denominator and Backlight, this book completes Finnish author Saisio’s autofictional trilogy. It covers her young adulthood in the 1970s, where she comes out as lesbian (“The electricity doesn’t go out. The Richter scale remains still”) and falls in love. One of her lovers, Havva, is a communist who’s engaged to a man; she relies on his rich parents for funding, but pees in their private pool as a protest. Later, Saisio is voted vice-president of a political drama company, as “she has the skills to bring about the revolution, specifically via theatre” – despite half-baked productions such as the “napalm opera” Vietnam-a-Go-Go. As that suggests, this is a story with a sense of both the ridiculous and the serious. Told in clear prose, it playfully shifts between third and first person as Saisio recounts her memories then analyses them. This enchanting series deserves to become a modern classic.

Short Circuit by Wolf Haas, translated by Jamie Bulloch (HarperVia, £20)

“We think [time] goes in one direction. But really you need to think of it as a loop”. This, well, loopy novel opens with jigsaw aficionado and “merciless hair-splitter” Franz Escher getting an electrician in to fix his power – then accidentally killing him. As Franz waits for the ambulance, he reads a novel about Elio, a man who helped put his own mafia family behind bars. Elio, who’s now on witness protection, kills time by reading a novel about … Franz Escher. The two stories pursue one another, accelerating until they collide, incorporating courtship by car alarm, rival funeral orators and multiple identities for many characters. Oh, and what if the electrician Franz killed turns out to be Elio? Short Circuit, recalling the slipstream fiction of Christopher Priest and the light-touch experimentations of David Mitchell, is an entertaining literary hall-of-mirrors.

Cosmos by Lucia Odoom, translated by Hunter Simpson (Daunt, £10.99)

“Lately my leap feels more and more like a fall,” writes Cosmos, a young Ghanaian man who has migrated to Copenhagen, where he contends with Denmark’s “worrying lack of smells” and collects recyclable bottles to earn money. Later he gets a job modelling, and lets the agency believe he’s an asylum seeker so they’ll feel sorry for him. He falls in love with Elizabeth: when she describes something as a guilty pleasure, “I asked her what a guilty pleasure was”. The past presses in: when Elizabeth takes him to the seaside, he recalls the vomit-streaked boat journey to Europe. All this is told in WhatsApp messages to Cosmos’s family back home – even the sex scenes. It’s a story of the challenges and hopes of a migrant’s life, made charming by the funny narrative voice and Cosmos’s optimism: he can see a plane and imagine being a crow, “flying high above the world, high above everything that no one owns”.

The Fallen Trees Are Also the Forest by Alejandra Kamiya, translated by Daniel Hahn (Pushkin, £12.99)

In this collection of stories from a Japanese-Argentinian writer, people rarely say what they mean. The dark secret beneath a woman’s meticulous breakfast preparations is hinted at through imagery: a flower, “open like a yelling mouth”. A story where a family attempts to cope when their son leaves by not talking about him (“I learned to differentiate between many different types of silence”) reads like an epic in miniature. There is black comedy – a woman asks her maid to help her read the letters on an optician’s chart – as well as intense psychological drama, in the tale of a soldier who is told to “dig here until further orders” and keeps going, and going, and going. Kamiya’s collection is remarkable in its variety but united by its laconic, sometimes elliptical style. These are teasing, satisfying stories to be savoured slowly.

entries.title: Ukrainian publishers call for support after Russian attacks destroy 10m books
entries.summary: The country risks ‘the collapse of the entire book ecosystem’ following destruction of warehouses in July and August, say Ukrainian publishersThe Ukrainian Book Institute has called on the international publishing community to support Ukrainian publishers after Russian attacks in July and early August destroyed about 10m books and a significant share of the country’s book production capacity.The i
entries.content:
The Ukrainian Book Institute has called on the international publishing community to support Ukrainian publishers after Russian attacks in July and early August destroyed about 10m books and a significant share of the country’s book production capacity.

The institute said the attacks on publishing, printing and warehouse infrastructure had left some companies at risk of financial collapse. A major attack on 1 August hit warehouses belonging to the RNK-Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv, destroying approximately 8m books, following July attacks in Kyiv which led to the loss of more than 1.5m books. In all, the recent attacks have led to the destruction of approximately 30% of the volume of books produced annually in Ukraine.

The RNK-Ranok logistics centre, which stores books for the company’s many imprints, is also the distribution centre for the national bookselling chain KnyhoLand, which runs 51 shops and several websites.

Along with the estimated 8m books lost, a further 600,000 school textbooks were destroyed. The total loss has been preliminarily estimated at almost 1bn hryvnias (£16.5m).

“At this stage, we face the risk of the collapse of the entire book ecosystem,” said Oleksandra Koval, director of the Ukrainian Book Institute.

The institute is asking for donations to support Ukrainian publishers, and is calling on the international publishing community to work with Ukrainian publishers and raise awareness about Russian attacks on Ukrainian culture.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and now occupies about a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

On 16 August, a Russian attack on Kyiv led to a fire breaking out at the Pochaina book market, destroying several rows of stalls, books and vendors’ property. The Pochaina market, founded in 1997, was once one of Ukraine’s largest book markets, with hundreds of stalls and books from more than 120 publishers.

The institute said the book industry was of “strategic importance” to Ukraine, preserving and promoting Ukrainian culture and giving the country’s voice a platform at home and abroad.

The Ukrainian government is developing support programmes for affected publishers and printing companies, including grants to restore equipment and compensation for property damage. But the institute said publishers’ losses could not be fully covered by state assistance.

“Against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing attempts to destroy Ukrainian identity, culture and history, Ukrainian publishing has a special mission,” said Olena Odynoka, deputy director for international cooperation of the Ukrainian Book Institute. “Supporting Ukrainian publishers today is not simply about preserving an industry. It is about defending Ukraine’s right to speak in its own voice and shape its own narrative in the world.”

The institute also called for an end to cooperation with Russian publishers and literary agencies, saying that solidarity with Ukrainian publishers was crucial to preserving cultural heritage that Russia was “deliberately trying to destroy”.

entries.title: The best books to read in August: new paperbacks from Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Salman Rushdie and Werner Herzog
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some wonderful new paperbacks, from a short story collection by a literary great to razor-sharp criticism*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Dream Count

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

Dream Count is billed as “a publishing event 10 years in the making”. Composed of the interlocking stories of four women, Chiamaka (“Chia”), Zikora, Omelogor and Kadiatou, it is also quintessential Adichie: ambitious, astute and powered by an accumulation of feather-light sentences that build to devastating weight.

The women are immigrants in the US. Chia, a travel writer, Zikora, a lawyer, and Omelogor, a former banker turned grad student, are Nigerian; Kadiatou, a hotel maid, is Guinean. Chia’s first-person narration establishes the novel’s melancholic tone: “I have always longed to be known,” she declares in the opening line, “truly known, by another human being.” Driven to reminiscing about past lovers during the Covid lockdowns, she passes her time “grieving what I did not even know to be true, that there was someone out there who had passed me by, who might not just have loved me but truly known me”. Her story gives way to Zikora’s, who is desperately trying to track down the boyfriend who abandoned her following a surprise pregnancy and whose own story morphs, with a sting of surprising sweetness, into a paean to the pull of motherhood. The narrative is then riven by the tragedy of Kadiatou’s story before being overtaken by Omelogor’s musings about her dissolute lifestyle in Abuja prior to quitting her high-flying career to undertake postgraduate research on pornography.

The novel threads together childbirth and pregnancy loss, abortions and hysterectomies, fibroids and female genital mutilation, sexual assault and sexual harassment, as if nothing less than the whole of female experience is within its scope. Yet at the same time it is painfully introspective, not only because it is set against the backdrop of the Covid pandemic, a built-in reminder of “how breakable we all are”, but also because it includes many moments – such as when, pondering one of her breakups, Chia muses about “how quickly mystery dissolves to dust” – in which one senses the subliminal gesture towards deeper traumas, the feeling of unbearable confinement alongside floating alienation, the hermetic numbness with which many of us experience grief. Sara Collins

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The School of Night

Karl Ove Knausgård

Karl Ove Knausgård’s Morning Star cycle may turn out to be even larger in scope than his six-volume autofictional bestseller, My Struggle. Four books deep, this gargantuan work of supernatural existentialism is an unsettling account of the occult phenomena that attend the appearance in the sky of a bright new star. Mysteries from the first three volumes include: who killed the musicians in the forest? What’s going on with the local wildlife? Why does no one seem to be dying any more? By the end of The School of Night, the most burning question may sound comparatively mundane: who is Kristian Hadeland?

Scattered references appeared in the saga’s first 2,000 pages. Kristian Hadeland was the 67-year-old man buried without mourners by doubting priest Kathrine Reinhardsen in The Morning Star (2021). In The Third Realm (2024), he was the sinister chap hitching a lift with Kathrine’s husband after the unloved man she buried is supposed to have died.

The School of Night offers another answer. Here, Kristian Hadeland is the author of a 500-page suicide note, and the misanthropic narrator of a compellingly nasty novel. From the remote Norwegian island where he’s preparing to end his life, Kristian sets down the story of how he got there, starting with his time as a photography student in mid-1980s London.

Young Kristian has a good eye and self-belief, even if – as a visiting professor suggests – his photos are “a bit dull. Without temperament.” Soon after arriving from Norway, he meets the enigmatic Hans, a Dutch artist into artificial intelligence, and Vivian, who is staging a production of Christopher Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus; he develops an uneasy friendship with the former and a hostile sexual relationship with the latter.

When Kristian is home for Christmas, he’s antagonistic towards his family, too. After his sister overdoses, he hears his father describing him as “a black hole … a narcissist, through and through”. Outraged, he returns to London, retreating into himself. Then a chance encounter with a homeless man sets Kristian on a path from near ruin to staggering glory.

Intimations of the supernatural give the saga much of its momentum and uncanny frisson. But can the mystery be indefinitely sustained? A lot is riding on Knausgård’s ability to deliver on the colossal promise of this sprawling epic. But for readers with the stomach, patience and faith to keep going, this work of millenarian fiction remains an object of fascination. Charles Arrowsmith

£9.34 (£10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Will There Ever Be Another You

Patricia Lockwood

Lockwood contracted Covid early, in March of 2020, when transmission was blamed on grotty fingers and every doorknob was suspect – the era of fruit bleaching and handwashing jingles. Will There Ever Be Another You is the tale of what happened next, inflicted on a fictional Patricia: aphasia, hallucination, migraines, amnesia, paranoia, relentless self-obliteration.

The result is cortical shrapnel – you can almost hear this book rattle when you open it. Lockwood’s title carries no question mark: it is prayer, punchline, eulogy, manifesto, nightmare, often all at once. Fragmentation is not a new mode for Lockwood (she was christened, after all, “the poet laureate of Twitter”). But it is one thing to disrupt, another to be disrupted. There is a new kind of anguish here, a longing for coherence.

The opening pages are where she comes closest. Hollowed by the loss of a child, an American family travels through Scotland, kept afloat by “pure itinerary”. A precious item is lost. Shortly afterwards, our heroine slips into fever. The treasure is returned; her mind is not. It feels like a dark enchantment, a faerie bargain. “It stole people from themselves.” Lockwood writes of her illness. “You might look the same to others, but you had been replaced.”

Delirium reigns. We wheel from Roland Barthes to Cabbage Patch Kids, via Anna Karenina and the “butthole cut of Cats” (classic Lockwood territory). But there’s a drum of obsession beating underneath the chaos. Doppelgangers, changelings, clones, dolls; photographs and synonyms – these pages teem with replicants and replication. The modus operandi of a virus.

Lockwood’s detonated form is evocative, but not especially innovative (Eimear McBride was doing a version of it more than a decade ago in A Girl Is a Half-Formed Thing). We need accounts of long Covid, and plenty more of them. But Will There Ever Be Another You feels auteurish, the literary equivalent of a Wes Anderson film: over-styled and perilously close to self-parody. A delirious in-joke. Beejay Silcox

£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The Ten Year Affair

Erin Somers

In Erin Somers’s The Ten Year Affair, Cora, a millennial mother, craves a bygone kind of passion from a bygone kind of man. Unfortunately for her, morality in 2015 is rigid and cynical, and instead of having the affair, Cora spends 10 years overthinking it, fantasising about it and discussing it with her potential lover, Sam – a playgroup dad who is “chief storytelling officer” at a mortgage start-up (yes, that’s his job title. They all have absurd jobs). The book presents itself as a comic take on the classic adultery novel and a send-up of a narrow, self-conscious group of downwardly mobile New Yorkers. I’d call it the midlife adultery story our entire generation deserves: a propulsive, witty takedown of insufferable hand-wringers who’ve managed to ruin even sex. Honestly, I couldn’t put it down.

Beneath the story runs the subtle undercurrent of familiar middle-age questions: do our lives have meaning? Where do we go after death? These themes are more explicit in Cora’s imagined conversations. Reading these exchanges, I wondered what lesson Cora and her cynical lot would take from their disappointing dramas. Would Cora grow more open to life’s imperfect joys, its corny pleasures?

I loved this razor-sharp, hilarious, finely observed novel, written with such withering exactitude. It is absolutely aware of itself, spare and brimming with subtext: a portrait of an anxious, loin-girding generation in middle age, chronically embarrassed at ourselves, at once afraid of and desperate for sensation. Or maybe that’s just the New Yorkers. Let’s say it is. Dina Nayeri

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Vera, or Faith

Gary Shteyngart

Shteyngart’s sixth novel is a lively, skittish Bildungsroman, shading towards darkness as it tracks the journey – literal, educational, emotional – of 10-year-old Vera Bradford-Shmulkin, an overanxious, over-watchful academic high achiever whose run of straight As has just been blighted by a B.

Always happy to show his workings, Shteyngart cites Henry James’s 1897 novel What Maisie Knew as the prompt for Vera, or Faith’s child’s-eye account of complicated adult affairs, although his gauche heroine bears a passing resemblance to the author himself as portrayed in his 2014 memoir, Little Failure. Friendless Vera lives with her rackety Russian-Jewish father, Igor (Shteyngart’s name at birth), who edits a floundering liberal arts magazine, her harried Wasp stepmother, Anne (who added the “e” in tribute to Anne Frank), and a boisterous younger half-brother, Dylan, who likes exposing himself to houseguests. But she also has (or possibly had) a Korean-born mother, long since vanished from the scene. Invisible Iris Choi plays the tale’s white whale or MacGuffin; the elusive hidden figure that Vera is determined to locate.

The eccentric Bradford-Shmulkins are lurching towards crisis, but they seem a model of stability when compared with the rest of the country, which reveals itself in unflattering flashes in the corners of the narrative. Shteyngart’s novel, we come to realise, plays out a decade from now, in a “post-democracy” USA where red state officials monitor menstrual cycles, self-driving cars shop their owners to the feds and the news platforms are abuzz with Russian disinformation.

Shteyngart’s ode to a good American in a bad America conspires to be, by turns, a rueful human comedy and a coming-of-age caper, a dystopian chiller and an espionage yarn. The colourful tale never satisfyingly hangs together; its component pieces tend to jar more than gel. But Shteyngart sets about his material with abundant energy and charm. He sketches a convincing caricature of a near-future USA and provides a stoical heroine that we can uncomplicatedly root for. Even in a degraded, compromised, up-is-down social climate, that has to be deserving of a solid B grade at least. Xan Brooks

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Vulture

Phoebe Greenwood

“Middle East on Fire: Israel positions tanks on Gaza border.” Journalist Phoebe Greenwood’s debut novel follows Sara Byrne, a freelance journalist in Gaza in 2012, who is reporting for a “pretty rightwing” British newspaper.

Vulture is a caustic study of what it means to report from a conflict, and particularly relevant to the current moment. It’s a knowing portrait by Greenwood, who was a freelance reporter in Jerusalem between 2010 and 2013, and later a foreign affairs correspondent at this newspaper. Her antiheroine visits a morgue, where the bodies of children, “dusted in sand and blood”, wear torn Spider-Man pyjamas. She narrowly escapes a bombed hospital, which is “running out of anaesthetic and even basic painkillers”. Still, her editor requires stories, and so she pursues increasingly dangerous lines of inquiry.

The title of the book is testament to its wry tone, and ultimately its position. In Byrne, Greenwood has created a particularly acerbic character, reluctant or perhaps unable to offer sincere emotions in the face of horrifying events. Her battle-weary sense of humour, however, cannot last, and Byrne’s mental state becomes increasingly unstable. She believes a bird – identified as a pigeon, but described more like a vulture – is tormenting her. Her eyes are yellow; she winces with pain when she walks. Greenwood handles this descent well; the narration remains jocular, even arrogant, meaning it never feels hackneyed.

Occasionally, Greenwood’s creative writing feels less successful than the news writing within it: the protagonist’s filed copy is sometimes clearer than the prose itself. But Vulture remains a remarkably skilful debut. Greenwood’s style is compelling and blackly comic; the story could not be more serious. Sophie Dickinson

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Discontent

Beatriz Serrano

Ambivalence towards working life is the subject of this tremendously entertaining debut novel. “I only come into the office to lower my air-conditioning bill,” says 32-year-old Marisa. She’s “head of creative strategy” in a Madrid ad agency. “That’s a big deal,” says a friend. “No,” Marisa replies, “it just sounds like one.” She kills time between projects by posting trolling comments on dismal YouTube videos. Eventually she faces the worst horror of all: a team-building retreat, which she ends up dealing with in a masterfully perverse way. There’s pain underlying her quips (“No one knows who I really am”), but her story is peppered with pithy insights into the modern workplace, and plenty of vivid characters, such as the friend who’s “had work done”. “I’m filled with plastic,” she tells Marisa. “I’m the Atlantic Ocean.” John Self

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Thriller

Bluff

Francine Toon

Toon’s second novel is set in St Rule, a Scottish coastal town with distinct similarities to St Andrews. In 2023, Cameron returns home on Christmas Eve; meeting old friends revives memories of his teenage crush, former classmate Joanie, last seen 10 years earlier at a calamitous end-of-schooldays party. His attempts to find her are met with vagueness, evasion and, finally, warnings off. A second narrative strand takes us back to 2013, and the 18-year-old Joanie. Adrift after her discovery that her boyfriend is cheating on her has ruined their plan for a year abroad, she falls in with an older couple. David and Erin welcome her, make her feel important and seem, for a while at least, to have all the answers. Skilfully handled themes of guilt, regret and adolescent confusion coupled with dark academia make for an insidious tingle of doom, although the rushed ending may leave some readers feeling shortchanged. Laura Wilson

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Short stories

Short stories

The Eleventh Hour

Salman Rushdie

The Eleventh Hour, a collection of five stories, seems intended as a kind of coda to Rushdie’s career. The stories are death-haunted. One of them is called Late; it’s an afterlife fantasy in which a Cambridge fellow, whose career has resembled both EM Forster’s (writing a great novel about India) and Alan Turing’s (helping to crack the Enigma code), dies and haunts a young Indian student named Rosa; what links them may be the buried crimes of empire. The Musician of Kahani replays Rushdie’s greatest hits: it is about a child born at midnight (“the approved hour for miraculous births in our part of the world”) who, aged four, abruptly becomes a gifted pianist (like the rock star Ormus Cama in The Ground Beneath Her Feet, playing air guitar in his cradle).

These stories are entertaining but not particularly strong. The Musician of Kahana leans pretty heavily on cliche: “the university of life”, “priceless art”, “finger on the pulse”, “the wedding of the year” … In the South is better: a deft, moving anecdote about two old men in Mumbai who bicker and needle one another from their respective verandas. One of them, Junior, dies in an accident. The other, Senior, despairs, until he comes to believe that “death and life were just adjacent verandas”. Oklahoma invokes Kafka; it is a metafiction about a young Indian writer and the older American novelist he admires, or perhaps more than admires – in cases of literary influence, the story seems to ask, who is writing whom?

“Our words fail us,” goes the final sentence of The Eleventh Hour. It is the conclusion of a story about a piazza – a public space – in which language, here figured as a human woman, is courted, usurped, ignored. Finally she screams and vanishes, at which point, the piazza’s buildings all crack: “The piazza is broken, and so, perhaps, are we.” Words have not yet failed Salman Rushdie, even if, in this self-consciously late book, the spectacular originality of his novelistic peak sounds more as an echo than as an urgently present voice. Kevin Power

£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

Frankly

Nicola Sturgeon

First, Frankly takes us back to a council flat in the former mining village of Dreghorn, Ayrshire. There, a young Nicola identified with tomboyish George from the Famous Five, worried constantly about her dad joining the swelling ranks of the unemployed, and broke up with her primary school best friend because she wanted to spend more time on her homework. She identifies the fundamental contradiction that would propel her: “Alongside shyness, crippling lack of confidence and a dreadful fear of failure was a burning ambition, a drive to succeed, a craving to be ‘seen’.”

There are some moments of bracing honesty. She reveals she came close to having a breakdown after giving evidence at the UK Covid inquiry. I can’t think of another politician of her stature who’d describe themselves on the floor of their home office, gripped by a panic attack as they struggled to edit a crucial policy document – in this case the Scottish government’s white paper on independence. And a lengthy passage on her pregnancy loss, in which she writes about her lingering guilt and shares the name she had chosen for the baby, Isla, is almost unbearably intimate.

It’s startling to read her account of the tension and hostility she claims characterised her relationship with Alex Salmond long before the public split that resulted from her government’s handling of sexual harassment allegations made against him by two civil servants. (These later formed part of his criminal trial on 13 counts of sexual assault, of which he was acquitted in March 2020.)

At one point, Sturgeon observes that “whenever a man is alleged to have done something wrong some people’s first instinct is to find a woman to blame”. Right enough, but there are also legitimate questions about how someone in a position of power and leadership could be so ignorant of someone as close to her as Salmond was. Neither does she explain why the women who brought the original harassment complaints against Salmond described being left without any support by the Scottish government she led.

She fails to reflect on how having a married couple at the very top of the SNP for more than a decade impacted the party, encouraging the apparently lax governance so many colleagues complained about. Nor does she address the lack of succession planning for her eventual departure. Despite the book’s promise of candour, it seems like Sturgeon is only willing to entertain her readers’ curiosity so far. Libby Brooks

£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

All the Way to the River

Elizabeth Gilbert

The first chapter of Elizabeth Gilbert’s much anticipated new memoir closes on a four-page love letter to Gilbert from her late partner Rayya, who, dead for five years, comes to her in a “visitation”. In Rayya’s voice, Gilbert calls herself babe, baby, or “sunshine baby” multiple times, emotes in all-caps, and grants herself permission to write the details of Rayya’s terrible, humiliating final year. “Let me just look at you for a minute,” “Rayya” says to Liz. “Look at your little rainbow eyes! Look at your sparkling tears! You’re so beautiful!” The letter is deeply self-indulgent and excruciating to read. “You’re going all the fucking way this time – all the way to the enlightenment.”

I believe that the dead are gone and that artists don’t need their permission to evoke them. But I was stunned that this solipsistic mess opens the book, because Gilbert is a terrific storyteller – Eat Pray Love, her memoir of self-acceptance and healing, was read by millions. So, I scrubbed the false start from my mind, reminding myself that great literature shows people as they are, which means that at some point in every good memoir, we should see the narrator being awful.

Even so, it takes discipline and restraint not to let one’s flaws harm the writing – restraint that it appears Gilbert no longer has. All through the book, she reminds us of Eat Pray Love’s success and tries to echo and relive what she learned back then: that she’s addicted to love, but she can thrive alone if she has her spiritual and creative practices.

But the prose is clunky (“an unhealed wound looking for someone to land on”) and full of preposterous flourishes, such as when an imagined Rayya says, in a poem at the end of the book: “I love it when you talk about me: it polishes me like a diamond.”

As a storyteller she shines brightest when she’s not curating, but displaying her mistakes, and mourning them. “I tried to drain all the love from Rayya into me before she died … I became a vampire”. And when, instead of simply emoting, she sits down to craft a scene, she writes transportingly. The last days of Rayya’s life, in a house with two of her exes, are funny, propulsive, raw and moving – Gilbert forgetting about herself to help her partner, who’s alone and helpless and terrified to die. Dina Nayeri

£9.34 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Literary criticism

Literary criticism

Authority

Andrea Long Chu

Andrea Long Chu stands accused of not playing by the rules, of appraising works of fiction as if they were essays or confessions rather than aesthetic objects. “It is true that I tend to treat a novel like an argument”, she writes in the introduction to Authority, a collection of essays and reviews published between 2018 and 2023 in outlets such as N+1, Bookforum and New York Magazine. Chu – who won a Pulitzer prize for criticism in 2023 – believes “all novels refract the veiled subjectivity of their authors”, and to pretend otherwise is to indulge a “pernicious form of commodity fetishism”. In her reviews, books betray their authors, invariably revealing some kernel of inadequacy – be it immaturity, myopia or just terminal dullness.

This approach borders on the psychoanalytical, and makes for fun reading. Chu diagnoses a case of “Munchausen by proxy” in Hanya Yanagihara, whose bestselling novels A Little Life (2015) and To Paradise (2022) are powered by “the misery principle”: “horrible things happen to people for no reason”, and the author is “a sinister kind of caretaker, poisoning her characters in order to nurse them lovingly back to health”. She notes a troubling tendency towards “infantile” idealisation of mothers and girlfriends in Tao Lin’s autofiction, and finds “something deeply juvenile” about the scatological motifs in Ottessa Moshfegh’s novels. Moshfegh’s medieval gore-fest Lapovona (2022), fails to shock, because “You cannot épater le bourgeois without an actual bourgeoisie”; “the leading coprophile of American letters” is trying too hard to convince us she’s not a prude.

These essays are essentially journeys – knotty and meandering, with moments of pithy, clarifying insight. If you can hold someone’s interest while figuring things out for yourself in real time on the page, you’re doing something right. Perhaps the true source of authority is companionable intelligence, and what we think of as sound judgment is just a function of familiarity – comfort in another person’s psychic skin. Houman Barekat

£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Philosophy books

Philosophy books

The Future of Truth

Werner Herzog

At 83, Werner Herzog is a living legend who can and does do precisely what he wants. Like the strange, enchanting films for which he is best known, Herzog’s seventh book defies the usual conventions of structure, narrative arc and the delineation of fact from fiction, even as it addresses the very subject of truth.

This slim volume sets out Herzog’s views on truth in a world where technologically enhanced falsehoods proliferate. These appear to be an elaboration of Herzog’s Minnesota Declaration, the 12 statements he made in 1999 at the Walker Art Centre in Minneapolis. Much like the declaration, The Future of Truth contains strong, gnomic opinions which include despising cinéma vérité because it obscures more than it illuminates, as well as a plethora of surprising sentences such as “rather die than wear a toupee”.

Two principles are central to Herzog’s idea of truth. First is the notion that seeking truth is a greater goal than finding it. As he puts it, “the quest itself, bringing us nearer to the unrevealed truth, allows us to participate in something inherently unattainable, which is truth”. The second is that bare facts can provide little more than a boring “accountant’s truth” that is less useful than what he calls “ecstatic truth” in helping people understand what’s really going on in life.

If anyone else had written The Future of Truth, I suspect they would come under critical fire for odd choices in structure, rambling, contradictory statements, and, to put it bluntly, taking the piss out of the reader. After all, Herzog devotes five whole pages to the histrionic plot of an opera just to demonstrate that when art forms contain concentrated, intense emotion, we “invest this preposterous kernel with the full array of our own feeling, so that it seems mysteriously genuine”. However, because this book is a collection of uniquely Herzogian mindfarts, it resists a panning. Michael Hofmann’s sparkling and inventive translation from the original German – a crypto-zoologist is described as “a ham sandwich short of a picnic” – somehow makes Herzog more Herzog in tone. Farrah Jarral

£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

entries.title: How I’ve Tried to Change the World by Alexei Sayle review – does protest make a difference?
entries.summary: The comedian charts his life in demos from 1960s Liverpool to 2020s London in this fiery and addictive bookAt 74, the comedian Alexei Sayle is approaching a dangerous phase for veteran British leftists: becoming a national treasure. Once described by special branch, in a surveillance file gleefully quoted in this memoir, as an “intellectual thug” who made “foul-mouthed comments about the royal fam
entries.content:
At 74, the comedian Alexei Sayle is approaching a dangerous phase for veteran British leftists: becoming a national treasure. Once described by special branch, in a surveillance file gleefully quoted in this memoir, as an “intellectual thug” who made “foul-mouthed comments about the royal family”, Sayle now appears regularly on Radio 4. His jolly, self-deprecating, man of the people side – one of his radio series is called Alexei Sayle’s Imaginary Sandwich Bar – has made him almost cosy.

But not quite. One fascination of his meandering career, which has included villainous Hollywood cameos, subversive podcasts and successful novelty pop songs, is the persistent fierceness of his politics – the underlying subject of this short, sharp book. “My decision to become … a professional funny man,” he writes, “wasn’t a choice made simply out of monstrous vanity … I was also … taking part in [Antonio] Gramsci’s war of position: attempting to get examples of communist thought on to Top of the Pops, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade and Doctor Who.”

Alongside such sometimes well-paid efforts to apply the culture war strategies of the late Italian Marxist, Sayle has also been on a lot of marches. The contrasts and contradictions between these two forms of activism – one repetitive but comradely, the other more glamorous but often isolated – are pondered, mocked and mined for anecdotes in these busy, digressive pages. From marching against American imperialism with his communist parents in Liverpool in the 1960s to marching for the Palestinians in London last year, Sayle richly conveys the mix of enthusiasm and doubt which anyone who goes on demos will recognise: “believing in the cause but also sceptical that protesting about it would be sufficient”.

He confesses to other complicated feelings about street politics. “I have always found it a sad thing to be alone on a demo, lonely in a crowd,” he writes. Then he describes watching protesters fight the police: “I didn’t join in but nevertheless experienced a tremendous rush of exhilaration.” With his bulging eyes and cannonball head, straining suits and air of menace, the Sayle who first became famous as a standup and a star of the boisterous sitcom The Young Ones in the early 1980s seemed like someone who could handle himself in a political pavement battle. But this book shows he is much less macho, constantly examining his own motives and often finding himself ridiculous, “a capering jester”.

In 1991, during one of his sporadic attempts at US success, he went to Hollywood with his wife for auditions. Beforehand, “we went out for a walk along Sunset Boulevard in the hot night,” he writes. “The pavement was deserted except up ahead … was a single figure. ‘I bet they’re British,’ I said to Linda. When we reached this solitary pedestrian it turned out to be Billy Bragg.” There is a beautiful absurdity and melancholy about these two mouthpieces of austere alternative Britain in the 1980s now wandering a seductively escapist part of California in a less politicised decade. Although, given the way the book flits cheekily between droll stories, polemic and fantasy, we can’t be completely sure this meeting actually happened.

There are other irreverent encounters with fellow radicals. The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf once held their annual congress in a small, suburban London flat where Sayle lived in the 1970s. To him at least, “Their main activity seemed to be smoking, staying up all night and reading foreign newspapers in cafes.”During the 1990s, he drifted away from activism, disillusioned by the left’s flagging momentum and distracted by his career’s proliferating demands. He is cutting about the left’s – and his own – frequent lack of focus and forward thinking. But then the 2003 Iraq war protests re-energised him: “There is something elemental, ancient and magical about … a huge crowd of one mind.”

Towards the book’s end, its tone becomes more consistent and serious. “I have marched on every Palestine demonstration since October 7,” writes Sayle, who is Jewish, and he has lost friends as a result. Like a good political pamphlet, this slim volume is fiery and addictive. Yet unlike a pamphlet, it shows how politics relates to the rest of life.

entries.title: The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef review – a bizarre tale of psychedelic toads and hair-raising treatments
entries.summary: A journalist investigates the unsettling world of a charismatic shaman and the people who trusted himWhich, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you d
entries.content:
Which, in your opinion, is the worst current cultural trend: social media influencers; unregulated wellness practitioners; macho manosphere posturers; psychedelic bores; cultural appropriators? The good news is that, with Octavio Rettig, the central character in Kimon de Greef’s The Ego Trip, you don’t have to choose between them. He’s all five wrapped into one objectionable package, and so much more besides.

The tale begins with the Sonoran desert toad, an improbable amphibian that spends most of its life hiding underground in the baking badlands along the Mexico-Arizona border, and has done so blamelessly for millions of years. Whenever it rains, the toads emerge from their hiding places to mate, laying strings of eggs wherever water has pooled.

There have long been fanciful tales of hippies getting high by licking toads, but these ones are the real deal: the world’s only known psychoactive animal. In the early 1980s, humans discovered that the toad’s poison glands secrete a venom that contains, among other chemicals, 5-MeO-DMT, a potent hallucinogen also known as the “God molecule”. The first known user squirted the glands of a toad that his dog caught on to the windscreen of his Chevy Sport, where the substance dried and he smoked it.

He wrote a manual describing “an overload of thoughts and perception, brief collapse of the ego, and loss of the space-time continuum”. It was, in short, a lot. The prospect enticed other users, and those included, two decades later, Rettig.

A troubled young man from Mexico, Rettig started smoking dried toad venom in the first decade of this century, and claims it helped him kick his crack cocaine habit. That was a time when popular interest in psychedelics was re-emerging after the long post-1960s winter, and many medical practitioners were wondering if these mind-altering chemicals couldn’t help patients who weren’t responding to their traditional treatments. Much of the focus had been on LSD, psilocybin and ketamine, but 5-MeO-DMT provided a whole new level of experience. The shatteringly powerful effect of the chemical was said to replicate the effect of years of therapy in just half an hour, which is clearly an attractive prospect for a psychedelic entrepreneur keen to maximise patient throughput.

Rettig was no pioneer in his enthusiasm for smoking toad. Instead, his contribution was to create a tradition for this new hallucinogen, thus giving it the kind of mystical authenticity that peyote, morning glory and ayahuasca gain among devotees thanks to their association with ancient Native American rituals.

The Seri people, who live between the Sonoran Desert and the Gulf of California, have suffered terribly both under the Spanish colony of Mexico, and the independent republic. By the time Rettig visited in 2011, there were just a few hundred of them left, living in squalid and trash-strewn villages, predated upon by drug cartels and plagued by addiction. Rettig adopted their chants, claimed their ancient toad-based tradition had been suppressed and was only now being rediscovered, and started presenting himself globally as a practitioner of indigenous medicine.

There may well be a medical case for treatment with 5-MeO-DMT, but it’s hard to see any argument for treating people with it the way that Rettig did. He offered huge doses with minimal screening, sometimes inflicting treatment forcibly. (In response to footage of him being aggressive to clients, he told De Greef: “I am open to acknowledge that some of my actions might be disturbing for most audiences, but this is a very deep therapeutic work.”) He engaged in sexual relationships with women after serving them toad, denied responsibility when patients died, and never seemed to learn from his mistakes. Rettig claims: “My work has been misunderstood, misinterpreted, and misused.” But it is an incredibly dark tale.

A different writer might have been tempted to go gonzo, to smoke toad himself, and to come back with stories of ego death, the space-time continuum and the rest of it, but Kimon de Greef mercifully avoids that temptation. A South African, he came to the story of Rettig not from the world of psychedelics but from researching wildlife smuggling, which gives him an unusually clear-eyed view of how grim these kinds of practices are.

A lot of the reporting for this book began life in the New Yorker, and it is as methodical, exacting, well-written and exceptionally reported as you’d expect. Fortunately, De Greef avoids the fate that can befall books based on American magazine articles that fail to break free of them, and really enjoys the extra space. He launches into entertaining digressions into how exactly the toads’ psychedelic powers were first discovered, into how pharmaceutical companies are harnessing 5-MeO-DMT for their own ends, introducing fascinating cameos, before he returns to the main story.

He is not a man for grand conclusions, but I challenge any reader not to see this highly enjoyable book as a parable for so much that’s wrong with the current economy. Everything from the undeserved authority of charlatans, to the rampant exploitation of the natural world, to the hiding of hyper-capitalism behind a shield of cod-mystical woo-woo: it’s all in there.

Rettig’s ultimate fate has been to be largely forgotten by the movement he helped to popularise, which has mutated and expanded at the speed of social media, with new influencers appearing and new markets opening. The toads, meanwhile, have become just another commodity to be exploited.
